review.pendingBody: This wording is taken from published guidelines but the study's practitioner has not signed it off yet. Ausculta is a prototype. It is not for diagnosis or treatment.
review.stepsWrittenByTeam: The step-by-step wording below was written for this app in plain language. It is a description of the technique, not a quote from the source. A practitioner needs to check it before it is used with patients.

confidence.PRIMARY: Read directly from the source document
confidence.SECONDARY: Confirmed through a summary of the source, not the source itself
confidence.UNVERIFIED: Not confirmed against an original source — treat with care

provenance.verifyNote: Needs checking against the original document before this is shown to patients.

safety.title: When to stop and get help
safety.lead: Learn these signs. They tell you when an asthma attack needs medical care.
safety.stopExercisesBody: If any of the signs below start, stop the exercise. Breathing exercises are not a treatment for an attack. They are never a replacement for your reliever medicine.

emergency.heading: Get medical help now
emergency.description: If any one of these is happening, do not wait to see if it passes.
emergency.action: Call your doctor or go to the nearest clinic now.
emergency.papppAction: Call your doctor or emergency room immediately. If you cannot reach anyone, take the patient to the nearest hospital right away.

worsening.heading: Signs your asthma is getting worse
worsening.description: These are the signs families are taught to watch for. They mean your asthma is worsening. Follow the plan your practitioner gave you and contact them.

nonAcute.heading: Do not ignore this one, even though it is not an emergency
nonAcute.description: This is not an asthma attack. It is a reason to get checked.

equipment.PULSE_OXIMETER: Only if you have a pulse oximeter at home.
equipment.PEAK_FLOW_METER: Only if you have a peak flow meter and someone has trained you to use it.

RELIEVER_NOT_HELPING.title: Your reliever inhaler is not helping
RELIEVER_NOT_HELPING.detail: You used your reliever the way your practitioner told you and your breathing does not ease within minutes.

CANNOT_SPEAK_FULL_SENTENCE.title: Too breathless to walk or talk
CANNOT_SPEAK_FULL_SENTENCE.detail: You cannot finish a full sentence in one breath. In a child under five, watch for not being able to speak or to drink.

CYANOSIS.title: Lips, face, tongue or nails look blue or grey
CYANOSIS.detail: A colour change like this means the body is not getting enough oxygen.

CONFUSED_OR_DROWSY.title: Confused, very sleepy, or hard to wake
CONFUSED_OR_DROWSY.detail: Being drowsy or muddled during an attack is a danger sign, not tiredness.

RETRACTIONS_STRUGGLING.title: Visibly struggling to breathe
RETRACTIONS_STRUGGLING.detail: Hunched over, using neck and chest muscles to breathe. The nostrils flare. The skin pulls in between the ribs, below the ribs, or above the collarbones.

VERY_FAST_BREATHING.title: Breathing much faster than normal for the age
VERY_FAST_BREATHING.detail: Count the breaths for one full minute at rest and compare with the table below.

SILENT_CHEST.title: The chest has gone quiet during a bad attack
SILENT_CHEST.detail: If the wheeze stops during a severe attack, that is a danger sign. It does not mean the attack is over.

FAINTING_DIZZY_COLD_SWEAT.title: Fainting, dizziness, or a sudden cold sweat

CHEST_PAIN_EXERCISE.title: Chest pain during or after exercise
CHEST_PAIN_EXERCISE.detail: Treat this as a possible heart emergency. Do not assume it is the asthma.

RELIEF_PERIOD_SHORTENING.title: The reliever helps for less and less time
RELIEF_PERIOD_SHORTENING.detail: Each dose wears off sooner than the last one did.

INFANT_REPEATED_RELIEVER.title: A baby under one year needs the reliever again and again
INFANT_REPEATED_RELIEVER.detail: Repeated doses in a baby this young need to be seen by a clinician.

CANNOT_TREAT_AT_HOME.title: You cannot treat the attack where you are
CANNOT_TREAT_AT_HOME.detail: The medicine or the equipment is not there, or the person caring for the patient cannot manage the attack at home.

OXYGEN_BELOW_92.title: Oxygen level below 92 percent while breathing normal air
OXYGEN_BELOW_92.detail: This is the level the Philippine pediatric guideline uses as a reason to go to hospital.

MORE_WHEEZE_AND_BREATHLESS.title: More wheezing and more shortness of breath
MORE_WHEEZE_AND_BREATHLESS.detail: The wheeze and the breathlessness are worse than they usually are.

FAST_BREATHING_RETRACTIONS.title: Fast breathing, flaring nostrils, or skin pulling in
FAST_BREATHING_RETRACTIONS.detail: The skin pulls in between the ribs, below the ribs, or above the collarbones with each breath.

MORE_COUGHING_AT_NIGHT.title: More coughing, especially during sleep
MORE_COUGHING_AT_NIGHT.detail: Coughing that wakes the patient at night is a sign the asthma is not controlled.

LESS_ACTIVE_TIRED.title: Less active, less energy, tires quickly
LESS_ACTIVE_TIRED.detail: Cannot do as much as usual, or gets out of breath sooner than usual.

DAILY_ACTIVITIES_AFFECTED.title: Everyday things are getting hard
DAILY_ACTIVITIES_AFFECTED.detail: Trouble with normal daily activities, including feeding in a small child. Being restless or irritable also counts.

POOR_RESPONSE_TO_RELIEVER.title: The reliever medicine is not working as well as usual
POOR_RESPONSE_TO_RELIEVER.detail: It helps less than it normally does.

SPO2_BELOW_94.title: Oxygen level below 94 percent
SPO2_BELOW_94.detail: This is one of the signs families are taught to watch for at home.

PEAK_FLOW_BELOW_80.title: Peak flow below 80 percent
PEAK_FLOW_BELOW_80.detail: Peak flow is a bonus check, not a requirement. It is never a replacement for a good clinical history and should not be relied on by itself.

COUGH_TWO_WEEKS_TB.title: A cough that has lasted two weeks or more
COUGH_TWO_WEEKS_TB.detail: With or without fever, weight loss, or blood in the spit. Ask about TB screening at your nearest DOTS or health centre. Do not put it down to asthma without being checked.

respiratoryRate.heading: How fast is too fast?
respiratoryRate.howTo: Count the breaths for one whole minute while the person is resting. You need no equipment for this.
respiratoryRate.tableCaption: Resting breaths per minute — the calm range used by the Philippine national plan
respiratoryRate.discrepancy: The same guideline gives slightly different numbers in its hospital-referral section (under 60 a minute for 0 to 2 months, under 50 for 2 to 12 months, under 40 for 1 to 5 years). The two lists do different jobs. The table above is the one written for patients and families. Your practitioner sets the number that counts for you.
respiratoryRate.notYourThreshold: This table is general information. It is not a number set for you. Only your practitioner can set the breathing rate that means something for you.

appBoundary.heading: What this app will not do
appBoundary.body: Ausculta cannot judge how bad an attack is, and it will never work out a dose or a diagnosis for you. What it can do is show you the warning signs and the plan and contacts your practitioner already wrote down.
appBoundary.fallback: Discuss this intervention with your healthcare professional.

plan.title: My asthma action plan
plan.lead: A written plan tells you what to do on a good day, on a bad day, and in an emergency. Your practitioner fills it in with you.

notAssigned.title: Your practitioner has not assigned a plan yet
notAssigned.body: Ausculta will never write an asthma action plan for you. A plan appears here only after a practitioner has filled it in and approved it. Ask your practitioner about a written asthma action plan at your next visit.

pendingApproval.title: A plan has been started but not approved yet
pendingApproval.body: Your practitioner has begun a plan but has not approved it. Until they do, it is not the plan to follow. Keep following whatever instructions they have already given you.

plan.notFilled: Your practitioner has not filled this in yet.
plan.emptyPlanTitle: This plan has no details in it yet
plan.emptyPlanBody: Your practitioner approved a plan but has not written the details in yet. Ask them to complete it at your next visit.

GREEN.name: Green zone
GREEN.meaning: Asthma is under control. No symptoms. Normal activity and normal sleep.

YELLOW.name: Yellow zone
YELLOW.meaning: A mild to moderate attack. Asthma is worsening. Symptoms have started or activity and sleep are affected.

RED.name: Red zone
RED.meaning: A severe attack. This is dangerous. The medicine is not helping.

plan.peakFlowOptional: Optional. The national plan treats peak flow as a bonus, not a requirement. Most clinics here do not have a peak flow meter.
plan.medicinesNote: Only a practitioner can write medicine names, doses, or puff counts. Ausculta will never fill these in.

contacts.heading: Who to contact
contacts.empty: Your practitioner has not filled this in yet.

redAction.heading: In the red zone
redAction.body: Call your doctor or emergency room immediately. If you cannot reach anyone, take the patient to the nearest hospital right away.

plan.templateSource: This plan follows the structure of the symptom-based Written Asthma Action Plan in the Philippine national pediatric asthma guideline. That guideline calls its own version a sample that practitioners should adapt.
plan.filledBy: Filled in by your practitioner on {{date}}
plan.reviewReminder: A written plan should be reviewed and updated regularly. Bring it to your next visit.

techniques.title: Breathing and exercise
techniques.lead: A short list. Each one here has evidence behind it and is safe for people with asthma. We would rather show you four we can stand behind than ten we cannot.
techniques.honesty: Be realistic about what these do. In adults, breathing exercises may help quality of life and hyperventilation symptoms, but probably not asthma symptoms themselves. In children the evidence is not strong enough to recommend them as standard care. No harm has been reported from breathing techniques in people with asthma.
techniques.universalCaution: None of these replace your reliever medicine during an attack. If you have any of the warning signs, stop and get medical help.
techniques.practitionerSets: Your practitioner decides whether an activity is right for you, how often to do it, and for how long. Ausculta does not set this.

evidence.STRONG: Strong. Backed by a strong, high-certainty recommendation in a national guideline.
evidence.MODERATE: Moderate. One good trial supports it, with real limits on what it showed.
evidence.LIMITED: Limited. Plausible and very low risk, but the direct asthma evidence is weak.

notOffered.heading: One activity we have deliberately left out
notOffered.body: The Ausculta specification originally listed huff coughing as a rehabilitation activity. We removed it. Here is why, so nobody adds it back by mistake.

HUFF_COUGHING.name: Huff coughing
HUFF_COUGHING.reason: Huff coughing is the forced-breath-out part of the Active Cycle of Breathing Technique. That technique is used to clear mucus in cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis and COPD. It has no asthma evidence at all. Physiotherapy sources list bronchospasm and twitchy, over-reactive airways as a reason not to do it — and asthma is a disease of over-reactive airways.
HUFF_COUGHING.rule: Ausculta will not suggest this to you. Only a practitioner can prescribe it, for a specific chest illness with mucus, and never during active wheezing. Ask your practitioner first.

PURSED_LIP_BREATHING.name: Pursed-lip breathing
PURSED_LIP_BREATHING.summary: Breathe out slowly through pursed lips, so the breath out lasts longer than the breath in.
steps: Sit up straight and let your shoulders drop.
Breathe in gently through your nose with your mouth closed.
Purse your lips, as if you were about to whistle.
Breathe out slowly and gently through your pursed lips.
Do not force the air out. Let it flow.
Stop whenever you want to. Stop straight away if you feel worse.
PURSED_LIP_BREATHING.suits: Teenagers and adults. It has also been used informally with school-age children. There are no trials made just for children, so a practitioner should decide if it suits a younger child.
cautions: This is not a treatment for an asthma attack and does not replace your reliever medicine.
Stop if your breathing gets worse instead of easier.
The direct asthma evidence is weak. Most of what is known about how it works comes from COPD, not asthma.

DIAPHRAGMATIC_BREATHING.name: Belly breathing
DIAPHRAGMATIC_BREATHING.summary: Breathe using the muscle under your lungs, so your belly moves instead of your chest.
steps: Sit or lie down somewhere comfortable.
Put one hand on your chest and the other on your belly.
Breathe in slowly through your nose. Try to make the hand on your belly move outwards.
Keep the hand on your chest as still as you can.
Breathe out slowly and feel your belly settle back in.
Keep your neck and shoulders loose the whole time.
DIAPHRAGMATIC_BREATHING.suits: Teenagers and adults. It has been used with children as part of larger programmes, but it has never been tested on its own in children.
cautions: This is not a treatment for an asthma attack and does not replace your reliever medicine.
Stop if your breathing gets worse instead of easier.
The direct asthma evidence is weak. It has not been tested on its own in the main review of breathing exercises for asthma.

BREATHING_RELAXATION_RETRAINING.name: Breathing and relaxation retraining
BREATHING_RELAXATION_RETRAINING.summary: Learning a calmer, gentler way of breathing, together with relaxing your body. This replaces the vaguer 'controlled breathing' and 'deep breathing' on the original list.
steps: Sit somewhere quiet. Let your shoulders, jaw and hands go loose.
Breathe in and out through your nose, not your mouth.
Breathe gently. Do not take big gulps of air — bigger is not better here.
Let your belly do the work, the way you did in belly breathing.
Try not to sigh or yawn between breaths.
Stay relaxed while you breathe. The relaxing is part of the exercise, not a break from it.
BREATHING_RELAXATION_RETRAINING.suits: Teenagers from about sixteen, and adults. The trial behind it included people aged sixteen to seventy. It has never been tested in children, so it is not offered as a children's activity.
cautions: This is not a treatment for an asthma attack and does not replace your reliever medicine.
Expect it to help how you feel, not how your lungs measure. In the trial, symptom scores and anxiety improved but lung function did not.
Stop if your breathing gets worse instead of easier.

EXERCISE_WARM_UP.name: Warm up before hard exercise
EXERCISE_WARM_UP.summary: A proper warm-up before hard exercise makes exercise-triggered asthma less likely and less severe.
steps: Before hard exercise or sport, warm up first. Do not start at full effort.
Build up gradually until your body is ready.
Both steady hard warm-ups and mixed-effort warm-ups have been shown to work, so use whichever your coach or practitioner prefers.
Tell your teacher or coach that you have asthma.
Follow whatever your practitioner has told you to do before exercise.
Stop exercising if your chest tightens or your breathing does not settle.
EXERCISE_WARM_UP.suits: School-age children, teenagers and adults who take part in PE or sport. This is the one item here with a strong, high-certainty recommendation behind it.
cautions: Chest pain during or after exercise should be treated as a possible heart emergency. Get medical help. Do not assume it is asthma.
A warm-up does not replace your reliever medicine or your action plan.
Stop and get help if any warning sign appears.

PAPP_2021.label: Philippine pediatric asthma guideline, 2021
PAPP_2021.source: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Pediatric Asthma 2021. Philippine Academy of Pediatric Pulmonologists, with the Philippine Pediatric Society and the Philippine Society of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology. The Department of Health sits on its consensus panel.

GINA_2023_POCKET.label: GINA 2023 Pocket Guide
GINA_2023_POCKET.source: Global Initiative for Asthma, Pocket Guide for Asthma Management and Prevention, July 2023.

GINA_2025_SUMMARY.label: GINA 2025 Summary Guide
GINA_2025_SUMMARY.source: Global Initiative for Asthma, Summary Guide for Asthma Management and Prevention, updated June 2025.

PAPWORTH_RCT.label: Papworth method trial
PAPWORTH_RCT.source: Holloway and West, randomised controlled trial of integrated breathing and relaxation training, Thorax. 85 adults aged 16 to 70. Symptom scores, dysfunctional breathing and anxiety improved at 6 and 12 months; lung function did not change.

STICKLAND_2012.label: Warm-up and exercise-induced asthma, pooled analysis
STICKLAND_2012.source: Stickland and colleagues, 2012, pooled analysis of 7 controlled trials, cited in the Philippine pediatric guideline (recommendation 9a.1, adopted from GINA 2021) as strong, high-certainty evidence.

NCCIH_2022.label: US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
NCCIH_2022.source: NCCIH consumer guidance on breathing exercises for asthma, reviewed March 2022.

COCHRANE_BREATHING.label: Cochrane review of breathing exercises for asthma
COCHRANE_BREATHING.source: The current Cochrane systematic review of breathing exercises for asthma.
COCHRANE_BREATHING.note: The project research synthesis refers to this review but did not record its full reference. The exact citation must be confirmed before this is published.

ASTHMA_LUNG_UK.label: Asthma + Lung UK
ASTHMA_LUNG_UK.source: Asthma + Lung UK patient guidance, reviewed 30 November 2023. States plainly that peak flow is not a substitute for a good clinical history and should not be relied on in isolation.

CDC_WHO_GINA_DANGER_SIGNS.label: Converged danger signs, CDC, WHO and GINA
CDC_WHO_GINA_DANGER_SIGNS.source: Danger signs that appear consistently across CDC patient guidance, WHO adult danger signs and the IMCI framework, and GINA.
CDC_WHO_GINA_DANGER_SIGNS.note: GINA's exact severity table could not be read from the original document during the project research. The signs themselves converge across sources; any numeric severity cut-off must be taken from a clean copy of the current GINA guide.

JOHNS_HOPKINS_CHEST_PAIN.label: Johns Hopkins Medicine
JOHNS_HOPKINS_CHEST_PAIN.source: Johns Hopkins Medicine guidance that chest pain during or after exercise should be treated as a possible cardiac emergency rather than assumed to be asthma.

DOH_NTP_WHO_TB.label: Philippine DOH National TB Program and WHO
DOH_NTP_WHO_TB.source: The two-week cough criterion used by the Philippine Department of Health National TB Program and by WHO to identify people who should be screened for tuberculosis. This is a screening prompt only, never a diagnosis.

ACBT_CONTRAINDICATION.label: Physiotherapy guidance on the Active Cycle of Breathing Technique
ACBT_CONTRAINDICATION.source: Physiotherapy sources listing bronchospasm and hyper-reactive airways as a contraindication to the Active Cycle of Breathing Technique, of which huff coughing is the forced-expiration phase.
ACBT_CONTRAINDICATION.note: The project research synthesis records this contraindication but did not capture a single named primary source. The exclusion decision stands on it, so a clinician should confirm the reference.
